newsitem.title: USA: "Fight fire with fire" in U.S. forests, Babbitt urges.
newsitem.headline: "Fight fire with fire" in U.S. forests, Babbitt urges.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt called on Tuesday for changes in forest management practices to counter a trend towards ever more disastrous wildland fires in the western United States.

Saying "we can learn to fight fire with fire," Babbitt called for prescribed fires and thinning out of young trees to reduce the intensity of the huge wildfires that sweep across western states every summer and fall.
Babbitt said his goal was to restore forests to the equilibrium that existed before Europeans settled the West.

"To restore health, character and structure to our forests...the obvious first step is to bring back their own ancient predator: wildland fire," Babbitt said in a speech at Boise State University in Idaho.

Last summer was the worst fire season in recent history in the West. Fierce fires ripped through tinder-dry forests, blackening huge areas. Thousands of firefighters battled them in a hugely expensive effort.

Babbitt said scientific evidence showed that in recent years "wildland fires in forests and on ranges have burned hotter, bigger, and faster, growing ever more lethal, destructive and expensive to fight." The United States was spending $1 billion a year to put out wildfires, he said.

Before the West was settled, light ground fires swept through forests every seven to 10 years, destroying undergrowth but leaving trees intact, Babbitt said. At that time there were only a few dozen trees per acre.

After the 1880s, overgrazing by cattle and sheep meant there was no longer enough dry grass in the forests to spread healthy natural fires, he said. For decades the policy was to suppress fires. Forests became far denser, contributing to the destructive fires of today, he said.

"By using all the tools we have -- carefully thinning excess young trees, igniting prescribed fires, managing land for fire, controlling invasive and exotic weed species -- we must take steps to reduce the fuels," Babbitt said.
